paras: The attempted lynching of John Andrew Johnson refers to repeated mob threats in June and October 1888 against Johnson, a nineteen-year-old Black man held at Crockett, Houston County, Texas, on a charge of raping a white girl. Officers moved him to Houston and later guarded the Crockett jail to keep him from the crowds, and he was legally hanged on December 21, 1888, after a conviction in the district court. Texas papers followed the threats as near misses, and the execution ran as a wire item across the country.

According to a Houston dispatch, a fourteen-year-old white girl, Olive Simms, the daughter of a farmer near Grapeland, was assaulted and left in the woods on the Wednesday before June 15. County officers pursued and captured Johnson, whom the Fort Worth Gazette called 'a negro', on the morning of June 14, and a Crockett special that day reported 'great excitement' and expected a lynching that night.

Johnson was jailed at Crockett, the county seat, but people from the girl's neighborhood gathered in the town during the day. Fearing an attack, the Houston County sheriff took him to the city of Houston on June 15, saying the Crockett jail could not withstand 'twenty angry and determined men'. On June 19 two men claiming to be a deputy sheriff and a constable from Crockett gave Sheriff Ellis at Houston an order for Johnson's delivery, until a telegram from the Crockett justice warned him not to hand over the prisoner. The Gazette supposed that Johnson would otherwise have been lynched.

After about two months in the Houston jail, Johnson was taken back to Crockett on October 5 for trial, and sixteen armed men were reported guarding the jail against a lynching. An Austin dispatch of October 11 said he had been convicted the day before of attempting to outrage the girl and that a large and growing mob surrounded the jail demanding him. In that account the sheriff barricaded the jail with eleven men armed with Winchesters and telegraphed for aid, and Governor Ross sent Adjutant General King to Crockett.

Johnson was hanged in the Crockett jail yard on Friday, December 21, 1888, protesting his innocence on the scaffold. The wire said the girl had recognized him and that three thousand people, 'mostly colored', watched the execution. No arrest of anyone in the June crowd, the Houston ruse or the October mob appears in the coverage.

The Fort Worth Daily Gazette carried most of the Texas coverage through special correspondents in Crockett, Houston and Austin. Its June reports called Johnson 'the Rape Fiend', 'a burly negro' and 'the colored rapist', treated the charge as proven, and headlined the threats 'ALMOST A LYNCHING' and 'A NARROW ESCAPE'. The October Austin dispatch instead stressed the guards' view that 'the law must be respected and upheld at all cost'.

The December hanging reached papers in Virginia, Tennessee, Minnesota and California under headlines such as 'Negro Ravisher Hanged' and 'Hanged for Rape'. Most versions noted his age and his denial of guilt, while the Sacramento Daily Record-Union placed Crockett in Louisiana.

A Crockett correspondent wrote on October 15 that the Austin reporter had 'got things rather mixed', that no troops had been sent or needed, and that Johnson's return caused only 'a ripple of excitement'; the rest of the letter is lost in the scan. The papers also disagree on the girl's name and age, from Olive Simms, fourteen, in June to Allie Simmons, seventeen, in December.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Andrew Johnson
bases: Crowds at Crockett threatened in June and again in October 1888 to lynch Johnson, held on a charge of assaulting a white girl, and officers moved and guarded him to prevent it; he was later legally hanged (A2, A5, A8).

No mob killed Johnson: officers kept him from the crowds (A2, A5), and he died by legal execution after conviction (A8, A11). The threatened mobs numbered 'twenty angry and determined men' or more and acted over a rape charge (A2, A5).

Several separate dispatches from Crockett, Houston and Austin agree on the charge, the June removal to Houston, the October return and threat, and the December hanging (A1, A2, A4, A5, A8, A11), though a Crockett letter disputes how serious the October threat was (A7).

accounts.label: Houston County sheriff (June)
accounts.gist: A lynching would certainly have occurred had Johnson stayed in the weak Crockett jail, so officers took him to Houston.

accounts.label: Houston dispatch (June 19)
accounts.gist: Two men posing as Crockett officers tried to get Johnson with an order; a telegram from the Crockett justice stopped it, and the paper supposed he would otherwise have been lynched.

accounts.label: Austin dispatch (October)
accounts.gist: A large, growing mob surrounded the Crockett jail demanding Johnson, and the sheriff with eleven armed men held it and asked the governor for aid.

accounts.label: Crockett correspondent (October)
accounts.gist: The Austin report was mixed up: no troops were sent or needed, and Johnson's return caused only 'a ripple of excitement'.

accounts.label: Crockett wire (December)
accounts.gist: Johnson was legally hanged for the June assault, recognized by the girl but denying guilt to the end.

framing.detail: The Fort Worth Gazette called Johnson 'the Rape Fiend' and 'the colored rapist' and stated the rape as fact, while framing the lynching threat as a near miss ('ALMOST A LYNCHING', 'A NARROW ESCAPE').
The October Austin dispatch quoted the guards that 'the law must be respected and upheld at all cost'.
The December hanging ran as a short wire under headlines such as 'Negro Ravisher Hanged' and 'Hanged for Rape' in papers from Virginia to California, several noting his protest of innocence.

conflicts.note: The June Houston dispatch is the closest to the event; the December wire gives a different surname and age.
The October Austin dispatch alone describes the conviction as for an attempt.

Threatened in June (crowd gathered, ruse at Houston); attempted in October per the Austin dispatch, disputed by a Crockett letter; no lynching occurred and he was legally hanged December 21
Never taken from custody; officers kept him in jail at Houston and Crockett
The threatening actors were crowds of citizens; officers protected the prisoner
Officers pursued and arrested him; the crowds threatened but seized no one
